narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimated a 52.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than passing, but not a certainty. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, well below the accepted-student average of about the sixth decile, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor, but it worked in your favor: at 3.30 it was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, pushing toward passing. Your first-year class standing was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure: third decile versus an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. Together, the two class-standing measures outweighed the positive signal from your GPA, so the model judged bar failure slightly more likely and the application was rejected.

Next, focus on strengthening the academic evidence that most affected this decision, especially your upper-year performance. Speak with admissions advising about whether additional coursework, a post-graduation record, or an explanatory addendum can address the low third-year standing. Ask what bar-preparation supports are available and consider a structured readiness plan before sitting for the exam. Because the estimate is close to even, a stronger recent academic record or persuasive context could materially change how a future application is viewed.
